title: The house with four doors
hook: Guru Arjan builds the Harmandir Sahib low in the pool with doors on four sides, open to all

segments.voice: Yesterday, Prithi Chand, and a Guru who answered with work, not revenge. Your line was pray for the difficult one.

Think about how important buildings are usually designed. They sit up high, on a hill or a platform, with a grand staircase and one main entrance, maybe with a guard. The meaning is clear: this place is above you, and you come in by permission, through the front. Now picture the pool at Amritsar that Guru Ram Das began. His son, Guru Arjan, finished it, and in the middle of the water he began to build a house of God. Almost every choice he made about that building turns the usual meaning upside down.
screen: `HIGH UP, ONE GRAND ENTRANCE.` → `THE POOL AT AMRITSAR.` → `A HOUSE IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WATER.`

segments.voice: It's called the Harmandir Sahib. Hari is a name for God, mandir means temple or house, and Sahib is a word of respect: the house of God. Many people know it as the Golden Temple, for the gold that covers it; that came much later, in the nineteenth century. First, instead of raising it high, Guru Arjan set it low. You walk down steps to reach it, so everyone who enters, rich or poor, comes down a little. Humility, built into the architecture. Second, instead of one grand entrance, he gave it doors on all four sides. In a world that sorted people by caste and by creed, this house was open from every direction, to everyone. Remember Guru Nanak's feet toward the Kaaba, and the question: which way is God not? Here's that question turned into a building. Tradition adds one more detail. Many Sikhs say the foundation stone was laid by a Muslim Sufi, Mian Mir, a friend of the Guru's from Lahore. Historians debate that story, but it has been told for a very long time, and it fits the house. The building was finished around 1604. It stands in the middle of the pool, reached by a causeway, and to this day the langar there feeds tens of thousands of people every day, of every faith and none. What Guru Arjan placed at its center is the story of the next few days.
screen: `HARMANDIR — THE HOUSE OF GOD.` · `SET LOW: YOU WALK DOWN TO ENTER.` · `FOUR DOORS, FOR EVERY DIRECTION.` · `A FOUNDATION STONE, TRADITION SAYS.` · then, large: `OPEN ON EVERY SIDE.`

segments.voice: If you can, get up and open a door, your front door, a window, the door to your room, and stand in it a moment, feeling the air come through. Think of who you'd welcome through it, and who you might have kept out without meaning to. Leave it open a while, if it's safe.
Harmandir Sahib. The house of God at Amritsar, set low in the pool with doors on four sides, open to all. Today's word.
Your line: open on every side. Four doors, one house, set low in the water. That's sixty days.

howItsDone: The Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar is the holiest gurdwara for Sikhs; visitors of every faith cover their heads, walk down into the complex, circle the pool, and eat together in its langar, which serves people day and night.

fork.setup: you're Guru Arjan, building a house of God in the middle of a pool. how many doors does it get?
options: no doors: only priests may enter.
fork.reveal: Guru Arjan gave it four doors, one on each side, so it was open from every direction, to everyone.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Harmandir Sahib, hari, God, and mandir, house or temple; also called Darbar Sahib, the Golden Temple.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Golden Temple, a beautiful landmark.
what it means: a house of God set low, so all come down to enter, with doors on every side, open to all.
what a scholar hears: begun around 1588, finished around 1604; the gilding came under Maharaja Ranjit Singh; Mian Mir laying the foundation stone is tradition that historians debate.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition (the building of the Harmandir Sahib; Mian Mir and the foundation stone)

notes: Dates: construction begun about 1588 (some say 1589), completed about 1604. Confirm.
Mian Mir laying the foundation stone: late tradition; many historians doubt it. Framed as 'many Sikhs say' and 'historians debate'. Confirm.
Gilding under Maharaja Ranjit Singh in the early nineteenth century: confirm.
Langar numbers ('tens of thousands every day'; often cited as 50,000–100,000): confirm before release.
Hari etymology: 'Harmandir' is often explained as 'Hari's temple'; confirm.
The installation of the Adi Granth (day 62) is not taught here; the close points at the next few days.
